summary: Lists requirements for a Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning protocol, including remote editing, locking to avoid overwrites, link management, simple metadata, container data types and versioning. It is informational and is a wish list, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo lists what a Web editing protocol would need so that several people can work on the same documents on a server without losing each other's changes. It asks for locks that keep a second person out of a document, a record of every saved version, and collections that act like folders. It is a list of requirements, not a protocol.

questions: what is the lost update problem
subtitle: What a Web authoring protocol needs: locks, versions, collections and properties for people editing the same documents.

tldr.problem: Web standards let a program fetch a document from a server and write it back, but two people editing the same page can silently overwrite each other's work, and there is no standard way to reach a document repository or version control system over the Web.
tldr.mechanism: This memo lists the features a Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning protocol must have: properties and links on any media type, write locks and reservations, collections, partial writes, and a version graph of frozen versions.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational. It records the WebDAV working group's requirements rather than defining a protocol, and its authors note that practical limits may make it impossible to satisfy all of them.

today: RFC 2291 is an Informational memo from February 1998 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the WebDAV working group's requirements for a distributed authoring and versioning protocol rather than defining one, so by itself it specifies nothing an implementation has to follow.

sections.title: Why Remote Web Editing Needs More Than HTTP
sections.content:
RFC 2291 records the requirements for a Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning (WebDAV) protocol, agreed by the WebDAV working group. It is not a protocol description. It is a list of features, each stated as a requirement with a rationale, that a later specification would have to satisfy.

The problem starts with what the Web already does. The Web lets a program fetch a document from a server with HTTP, let a person edit it, and send it back. That is enough for one author. It is not enough for several people working on related documents at the same time. The RFC's name for the result is the lost update problem: two people fetch the same page, both edit it, and the second save silently replaces the first person's work.

There is a second gap. Tools that want to reach a document repository or a version control system over the Web have had to use non-standard extensions to HTTP, so each product forces its own interface on the client and the extensions do not interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: The Web already lets a person edit a document that sits on a server. What it cannot do is stop two people from editing the same document at once and overwriting each other. This memo lists the features a protocol would need to fix that, and to keep a history of saved versions. It is a requirements list, not a protocol.

sections.title: Principles the Extensions Should Follow
sections.content:
Section 4 sets out eight principles that cut across all the features. User agent interoperability requires that any WebDAV client work with any WebDAV server, at least at a basic level. Client simplicity asks for a design that is easy to implement. Legacy client support requires a WebDAV server to understand any valid HTTP 1.1 request from an ordinary browser and to answer with a response that does not require the client to understand the extensions.

Two principles cover how data and systems are treated. Data format compatibility says servers should work with existing resources and URIs, and that extra information should not become a mandatory part of document formats. Replicated, distributed systems requires the extensions to work when version trees are split across servers, when collections hold members on different servers, and when any resource may be cached or replicated.

The last principles shape the protocol itself. Parsimony in client-server interactions asks for the fewest round trips needed for common tasks, such as publishing a document together with its properties or finding which resource in a version graph is the published one. Changes to HTTP recognises that WebDAV adds properties, collections and version graphs, so existing methods such as DELETE and PUT have to behave in well-defined ways in the enlarged environment. Alternate transport mechanisms notes that requests might one day travel by email, and that the specification should not rule that out.
sections.plainLanguage: The extensions have to work with today's Web software, keep the extra information out of the document formats, and survive being spread across several servers and copies. They also have to keep the number of requests between client and server small, and they have to say what existing HTTP methods such as PUT and DELETE now do.

sections.title: The Requirement Categories
sections.content:
Section 5 lists the functionality to be standardized, in twelve categories: properties, links, locking, reservations, retrieval of unprocessed source, partial write, name space manipulation, collections, versioning, variants, security and internationalization.

Properties are named descriptive pieces of information about a resource, such as author, title, publisher or subject. They must be creatable, readable, modifiable and deletable on resources of any media type. Links are typed connections between resources. The HTML LINK element already provides them for HTML, and the RFC wants the same support for bitmap images and other non-HTML media types.

Retrieval of unprocessed source asks that the source of a resource be available to any principal with authorization to edit it. A GET may return something other than what the server stores: server-side include directives, SGML source converted on the fly into HTML, or a word processor's native format converted into HTML. Retrieving the source returns the stored form instead.

Partial write asks that a client be able to send only the changes it made rather than retransmitting the whole resource, so that a one-character spelling correction does not require resending a large document over a slow link. Name space manipulation requires copy, which duplicates a resource on the server without the client loading and resaving it and leaves the two independent afterwards, and move or rename, which changes a resource's location without a load and resave and makes the old location unreachable. Moving and renaming are the same operation.

Collections are resources that contain other resources, directly or by reference. They must be listable, creatable, and have members added and removed. Where a URL level maps to a collection, such as a directory in a filesystem, the server lists its contents; where it does not, the server may answer with a 405 Method Not Allowed status code. Variants cover several representations of one resource, including different file formats and different languages.
sections.plainLanguage: Any resource needs properties such as author and title, and typed links to other resources, and both must work for any kind of file, not just HTML. A client must be able to send just the part of a document it changed. The server must be able to copy, rename and list files itself, so that a client does not have to download and upload a file to move it. Containers of resources, called collections, must be creatable and listable.

sections.title: Locking and Reservations
sections.content:
Locking is the answer to the lost update problem. A write lock prevents anyone other than its owner from modifying the resource it applies to. The RFC sets two general principles. A lock must be possible without fetching the resource and without committing to edit it, and it must be possible to lock several resources on one server in a single atomic action, so that either all of them are locked or none is. That matters when two people try to lock the same set at once: one of them gets the locks, and they cannot end up each holding part of the set.

Three functional requirements follow. A write lock must be able to restrict modification of a resource to a specific person. It must be possible to find out whether a given resource has active locks and, if so, who holds them. It must be possible to remove a lock.

Reservations are separate from locks. A reservation is a declaration that someone intends to edit a resource, so that other people can find out who is about to work on it. Reservations carry no access restrictions, and a lock does not imply that the resource will actually be edited. A principal must be able to register an intent to edit, ask who currently holds reservations on a resource, and release the reservation. Configuration management systems have shown that people need to know they are about to enter a parallel editing situation, so that they can coordinate by telephone or in person. A typical check-out combines a write lock, a reservation and a retrieval into one atomic operation, and a check-in combines writing the new version, releasing the lock and releasing the reservation.
sections.plainLanguage: A lock tells the server that one person is the only one allowed to change a document, so a second person's save is refused instead of overwriting the first. It must be possible to take the lock without first downloading the document, and to lock several documents in one step that either succeeds for all of them or for none. A reservation is weaker: it only says who plans to edit, and it does not stop anyone else.

sections.title: Versioning and the Version Graph
sections.content:
Most versioning systems record the history of a document by making each version frozen and unchangeable: a later change creates a new version rather than editing the old one. A client must be able to tell that a version has been frozen, and any successful retrieval of a frozen version must return exactly the same content, or an error if that version or the resource is no longer available.

The RFC's model is a version graph: a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are resources. Each version stands in a derived from relationship to its predecessors. One version can be derived from several, which is merging, and several can be derived from one, which is branching. The related versions therefore form a graph rather than a line. A single resource may take part in more than one version graph.

The functional requirements cover how a client names and finds these things. There must be a way to refer to a version graph as a whole, because operations such as moving a whole graph or asking for its history apply to the graph rather than to one member. Each member must itself be a resource, so that a link can point at one version and a client can ask for one version to edit. A client must be able to tell whether a resource is a plain resource, a graph, or a member of a graph. There must be a server-defined default member that the server returns for requests that name no version, which is the simplest way to keep clients that know nothing about versioning working.

Given one member, a client must be able to discover and reach the root member of the graph, its predecessors, its successors and the default member, and must be able to retrieve the complete topology of a graph in a standardized format. A client may propose a version identifier for a new member, though the server may refuse it and must then report the identifier it did assign; identifiers must be unique within a graph. A client must be able to attach version-specific properties to a new member, at minimum a comment explaining what changed, and must be able to ask the server which versions are locked, which are reserved for editing, and by whom.
sections.plainLanguage: Each saved version is kept unchanged, and later edits create a new version, so the history stays accurate and old links keep working. The versions of a document form a graph rather than a list, because one version can be merged from several and can lead to several others. A client must be able to name a version, find the versions before and after it, and ask for the whole shape of the history.

sections.title: Security, Internationalization and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC asks the WebDAV specification to state how its extensions interact with existing authentication schemes and to recommend which of those schemes to use. Access control requirements are left to a separate work in progress. The specification must also carry a minimal list of security protocols that any compliant client and server must support, so that the authenticity of messages is assured and their privacy and integrity are protected in transit.

Internationalization is treated as a requirement rather than an afterthought. Because authoring happens across languages, information intended for people to comprehend must conform to the IETF character set policy, which covers character sets, encodings and language tagging. The information covered includes not only the content of resources but also display names and descriptions of properties, property values and status messages.

The memo is a set of requirements, not an implementation, and it says so. As much as possible the functionality is described without suggesting a proposed implementation, because there are many ways to perform it within the Web framework and a single mechanism might satisfy several requirements at once. The authors also warn that practical considerations may make it impossible to satisfy them all, and that the working group's intention was to come as close as possible to doing so.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol must state how it works with existing authentication and must carry a minimum list of security protocols. Anything a person reads, including property labels and status messages, has to follow the IETF rules on character sets and language tagging. The memo deliberately leaves the mechanism open: it says what the protocol has to do, not how.

items.title: Properties
items.text: Named facts about a resource, such as author or title.

items.title: Links
items.text: Typed connections between resources of any media type.

items.title: Locking
items.text: A write lock keeps other people out of a resource.

items.title: Reservations
items.text: A notice that a person plans to edit a resource.

items.title: Partial write
items.text: Send only the part of a document that changed.

items.title: Collections
items.text: Containers for other resources, like folders.

items.title: Versioning
items.text: Frozen versions recorded in a version graph.

items.text: Authentication, access control and transport protection.
